newsitem.title: USA: Second week of jury selection starts in Broin case.
newsitem.headline: Second week of jury selection starts in Broin case.

text.p: A woman whose husband and father died recently from smoking-related cancers and another who said she did not believe secondhand smoke causes disease were added to list of jurors passing initial muster on Monday in a landmark $5 billion lawsuit against the tobacco industry.
Jury selection was sluggish at the beginning of the second week of trial in the closely watched class-action lawsuit, with just 19 candidates questioned and only five added to the pool.

The lawsuit, known as Broin v Philip Morris et al, seeks damages from nine tobacco companies and industry groups on behalf of some 60,000 flight attendants who say they were sickened by secondhand smoke on U.S.-based passenger jets.

After admitting 32 of the first 75 prospective jurors questioned last week, Dade County Judge Robert Kaye hoped to speed the process, ruling Friday that the candidates should be questioned in groups of six.

But early Monday he decided to continue the questioning individually when lawyers expressed concern that prejudicial statements uttered by one candidate could taint all six and lead to their exclusion.

Admissions brought the pool of prospects to 37 but because each side will be able to exclude 27 without explanation, the pool must be at least 60 to seat a panel of six, plus additional candidates to serve as alternates.

Among those accepted on Monday was a truck driver who opposed the smoking ban on U.S. domestic airline flights and said he believes flight attendants who thought their work environment was unhealthy should have sought other work.

The man, a smoker, also said he believed that the flight attendants' lawsuit "doesn't hold water." He was accepted over the objections of the flight attendants' lawyers, who called it a "clearcut case" of someone who should be excluded.

Kaye also admitted into the pool an unemployed restaurant worker who said her two-pack-a-day habit helped calm her nerves. The woman said her father and husband both died of cancer within the past four years. Both were heavy smokers and in both cases, doctors said smoking was a contributor to their deaths.
Asked if she blamed cigarette companies for their deaths, she said: "To be honest, I'm not sure." Neither side objected to her inclusion in the pool.

Another woman who was accepted over the objections of plaintiffs' attorneys said she did not believe secondhand smoke caused cancer and thought the flight attendants were "behind the eight ball" in the lawsuit.
Kaye excused one potential juror who said he had strong opinions against cigarette smoking and thought it would be unfair to put him on the jury.

Another possible juror, a former firefighter, said he believed secondhand smoke had negative health effects and contended that tobacco companies would have to prove to him that secondhand smoke did not cause disease.

Tobacco lawyers asked that the man be excused because he had effectively reversed the burden of proof. Under law, the plaintiffs will be required to prove that secondhand smoke causes disease. The juror was excused.

One jury candidate, excused by the judge after questioning, indicated on his questionnaire that he did not understand English very well. Kaye had expected language to be a problem in a county where Spanish is spoken in a majority of households.
